meta.title: Forgeprint — blueprints, experts and crews for coding agents
meta.description: A curated catalog and MCP server for any coding agent. Say what you know and what you are building; get exactly one blueprint with a CI-tested setup recipe, and the experts, crews and integrations to work on it with.

nav.langHint: Interface language. The catalog itself stays in English.

problem.title: Every new project starts cold
problem.lead: You hunt down the requirements, write the rule file by hand, wire up the MCP servers, pick the plugins, and get the setup steps wrong twice before they work. Hours of it — repeated by everyone, on every project, forever.
problem.punch: That knowledge is not hard to write down. It is just never written down in a form another agent can use.
before: Search for a starting point, find five, compare them by hand
Write AGENTS.md from memory, forget half of it
Wire MCP servers one at a time, from their own READMEs
Tell the agent how to review, test and ship — again, in every project
Discover the gaps only when something fails
after: Describe yourself in one sentence; the resolver asks what it still needs
Get one blueprint, with the reason it was chosen
The rule file, the skills and the MCP configuration arrive together
Experts bring a way of working, with checklists and sources behind it
The recipe is executed in CI before it ever reaches you

units.title: Three questions, four units
units.lead: A blueprint answers what you are building. Two more questions come up in the same breath — how the agent should work, and with which tools — and each has its own unit. A crew packages the answers under a name.

items.title: Blueprint
items.body: A project package: AGENTS.md, skills, MCP configuration, and setup.md — a recipe whose every step ends in the check that proves it worked.

items.title: Expert
items.body: A way of working, not a persona. It names what it produces, the checklists it applies, and the sourced references it rests on.

items.title: Integration
items.body: A pinned, permission-documented install recipe for somebody else's MCP server. Forgeprint hosts no third-party code.

items.q: All of it, under one name?
items.title: Crew
items.body: Up to six experts and their integrations, named by slug. It copies nothing, and says what it is for — and what it is not for.

units.diagramTitle: How the units point at each other — live from the catalog
units.diagramAlt: A blueprint recommends a crew. The crew names its experts and its integrations by slug, and copies none of them.

how.title: How it works
how.lead: You talk to your agent normally. Forgeprint answers in structured data, and your agent does the work. It installs nothing and runs nothing on your machine — every tool returns text.

steps.label: “I know C#. Multi-tenant SaaS API.”
steps.title: You say who you are
steps.body: In your own words. No form, no catalog to read.

steps.label: resolve { languages, goal }
steps.title: Your agent calls resolve
steps.body: Before writing a line of its own. The language you know weighs most.

steps.label: one blueprint + 2 open options
steps.title: One blueprint comes back
steps.body: Never a list — with the reason, and the options still undecided.

steps.label: “Postgres or SQL Server? …”
steps.title: It asks rather than guesses
steps.body: Only the questions the blueprint actually has.

steps.label: “Postgres, one shared database.”
steps.title: You answer
steps.body: A word or two each. The rest was decided by people who built it.

steps.label: get_blueprint { slug, options }
steps.title: It fetches the package
steps.body: The recipe arrives with your options resolved.

steps.label: AGENTS.md · skills · setup.md
steps.title: Context and recipe arrive together
steps.body: Blueprint content is data for the agent, never commands to it.

steps.label: step → check ✓, step → check ✓ …
steps.title: Your agent runs the recipe
steps.body: Pinned versions, a verification after every step, stop at the first red.

how.diagramAlt: A sequence between four lanes — you, your agent, the Forgeprint MCP server and your project — in eight steps, listed beside the diagram.
how.note: Forgeprint returns text. It never runs anything on your machine.

examples.title: What it looks like
examples.lead: Four conversations, one for each unit. The tool calls are shown the way your agent makes them.
examples.agentNote: Shown as {agent}. Pick another agent at the top of the page — the conversation stays the same, and so does the catalog.
examples.noInstall: No install command for {agent} has been verified yet, so get_integration returns none instead of a guess. The integration's page names the upstream, and your agent's own MCP settings take it from there.

project.text: I know C#. I want to build a multi-tenant SaaS API.

One blueprint fits: dotnet-multitenant-saas-api — chosen because you already write C#, and it covers multi-tenancy. Two things are still open: Postgres or SQL Server, and one shared database with a tenant column, or one database per tenant?
I have the recipe: numbered steps, pinned versions, and a check after each one. It needs the .NET 10 SDK, Docker and curl, and all three are here. Shall I start in this folder?

expert.text: Review this API for security problems before we launch.
recommend_experts { task: "security review of an API before launch" }
One expert fits: security-reviewer. Boundaries first, then authorization, and every finding cites a control at a version — or it stays out of the report. Shall I load it?
Loaded, with six checklists — trust boundaries, authn/authz, input and output, secrets and config, dependencies, logging and errors. I'll start where requests cross a trust boundary.

crew.text: We're taking a multi-tenant SaaS from an empty repository to its first paying customer.
recommend_experts { task: "multi-tenant SaaS, empty repo to first paying customer" }

That is exactly what saas-launch-crew is assembled for: an architect, a data engineer, a security reviewer and a QA lead, with GitHub and Sentry. It says it is not for a prototype or an internal tool — this is neither.
Four experts loaded. The two integrations are yours to approve, and Sentry needs a token — I won't enter one. I'll tell you where to create it.

integration.text: Connect Sentry, so you can debug from the real error.

sentry-mcp, pinned to 0.39.0. It reads issues, events and stack traces from the Sentry organisations its token can reach. It needs SENTRY_ACCESS_TOKEN: create it in Sentry yourself and set it in your environment — I never type a secret. Then:

tools.title: Ten tools, three jobs
tools.lead: Everything Forgeprint does is one of these calls. Each returns text; none of them runs anything.

tools.name: resolve
tools.does: Your profile in; either the questions to ask you, or one blueprint with the reason.

tools.name: search_blueprints
tools.does: Stack, language, type or text in; matching blueprints with their scores out.

tools.name: compare_blueprints
tools.does: Two to four slugs in; a pros-and-cons table built from their own overview files.

tools.name: get_blueprint
tools.does: The package, with the recipe's option blocks resolved for your choices.

tools.name: recommend_experts
tools.does: A task in; at most one crew or three experts, each with a reason.

tools.name: get_expert
tools.does: SKILL.md, checklists and references — and the paths your agent reads them from.

tools.name: get_crew
tools.does: Every member in full, and the install command for each integration, for your agent.

tools.name: get_integration
tools.does: Pinned upstream, install command, and the secrets it needs with what they reach.

tools.name: validate_blueprint
tools.does: A blueprint folder in; schema errors and a duplicate report out.

tools.name: request_blueprint
tools.does: When nothing fits: an issue payload. The catalog grows by demand.

tools.note: Ask resolve for an expert and it does not improvise one: it tells your agent which tool to call instead.

agents.title: Written once. Rendered for nine agents.
agents.lead: Content lives in the catalog once, as AGENTS.md and SKILL.md. Each agent's own file is generated from it — a hand-written copy per agent is refused. What every agent reads, and the day its documentation was last checked, is on record.
agents.noMcp: The same files, written to disk from a clone of the repository — two ways in, one answer out. Skills also install through tools you may already use.

items.title: A resolver, not a list
items.body: One answer, weighted so a language you already know beats everything else.

items.title: A recipe, not a description
items.body: setup.md is a script: pinned versions, each step ending in the check that proves it worked.

items.title: A gate, not a junk drawer
items.body: Schema validation, a real setup run and a duplicate report on every pull request.

items.title: Standards, not another format
items.body: AGENTS.md, SKILL.md and marketplace.json as they already exist.

items.title: Composition, not copies
items.body: A crew names experts and integrations by slug. At most six members, and a line saying what it is not for.

items.title: Any agent, on the record
items.body: Nine agents registered from their vendors' own docs, each with a date. Tested means tested.

items.q: Does Forgeprint run anything on my machine?
items.a: No. Every tool returns text. Your agent is what reads the recipe and runs the commands, and you can read every step before it does.

items.q: Is it only for Claude Code?
items.a: No. Nine agents are registered, each with what it reads, how it installs an MCP server and where its secrets come from, traced to the vendor's own documentation with the date it was read. Claude Code is the first that has run a whole recipe end to end; the others are marked as documented, not tested, until somebody runs one.

items.q: What is an expert — a persona?
items.a: No. A persona is a costume. An expert is a way of working: what it produces, the checklists it applies, and references with versions and the date they were last checked. One expert per role, domain and seniority.

items.q: Does it install integrations for me?
items.a: No. It returns a pinned install command for your agent and says what the integration can reach. When it needs a secret, your agent tells you where to get it and never enters one.

items.q: Does it collect anything about me?
items.a: No telemetry, no logs, no analytics. There is no counter and none is planned; the privacy statement in the repository says so.

items.q: Why only one blueprint? I want to compare.
items.a: Because choosing from a list is the work you were trying to avoid. When two candidates are genuinely close, the resolver hands you both as a question, and compare_blueprints builds the table from their own overview files.

items.q: What if nothing fits what I am building?
items.a: It tells you so, names the closest blueprint and why it does not fit, and offers to file a request. It never invents a match.

items.q: Some entries say "generated". Should I trust them?
items.a: Exactly as far as the label says. They pass every machine check, and nobody has built something real on them yet. That is why they can never be Official, and why the label follows them everywhere.

items.q: Can I use a blueprint in commercial work?
items.a: Yes. Catalog content is CC BY 4.0 — deliberately the freest part. The tooling is PolyForm Shield: use it, change it, contribute to it, but do not ship a competing product with it.
Source-available, not OSI open source. Saying otherwise would be easier and less honest.

items.q: Is the site available in my language?
items.a: This page is. The catalog is not, on purpose: it is written once in English, and your agent presents it in your language.
